mainEntity.name: What happens after a cancer diagnosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Our oncologists will review your pet's case, discuss treatment options, and create a personalized plan. We focus on quality of life and work closely with your primary vet. Many pets maintain a good quality of life during treatment.

mainEntity.name: What are signs of cancer in pets?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cancer signs vary widely but may include lumps, sores that don't heal, weight loss, decreased appetite, difficulty eating/swallowing, breathing problems, lethargy, or changes in bathroom habits. Early detection improves treatment outcomes.

mainEntity.name: What if my pet requires surgery for cancer treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: If surgery is necessary, rest assured our surgical department is well-equipped to handle all types of surgical oncology.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my pet is in pain during cancer treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Our team closely monitors comfort levels and provides appropriate pain management. We'll teach you to recognize signs of discomfort and maintain open communication about your pet's quality of life.
Most pets tolerate chemotherapy well with minimal side effects. Unlike humans, pets typically experience milder reactions to chemotherapy. We use lower doses and carefully monitor for side effects.

mainEntity.name: What is stereotactic radiation for animals?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT) is a highly targeted form of radiation that uses advanced imaging to deliver radiation with pinpoint accuracy, often in fewer sessions than conventional radiation treatments. This is particularly useful for tumors that are difficult to treat with traditional methods or are located near sensitive structures. It allows for higher doses of radiation to be delivered to the tumor while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue.

mainEntity.name: Does my pet need to undergo general anesthesia for radiation treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Yes. If not delivered where intended, radiation can be dangerous. Our treatments are executed precisely within 1-5 millimeters while the radiation beam is on. Therefore, for patient safety we need to ensure that patients are completely still during treatment. 
However, we only need them to remain still for 15-30 minutes. So we only use short acting or reversible anesthetic agents to ensure patients are able to recover quickly and not have their quality of life impacted at home.

mainEntity.name: Will my pet become radioactive or experience pain during radiation?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Pets do not experience pain or radioactivity with radiation treatments. 
The most common type of radiation utilized in veterinary medicine is high-energy x-rays. Not only is it not painful, but it is not stimulating in any way. You can think of how you felt if you have ever had an x-ray on a part your body.
Despite the name, radiation treatments do not lead to your pet becoming radioactive. You can feel free to interact with your pet as you wish before and after treatment.

mainEntity.name: Will my pet need to stay overnight during treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most oncology treatments are outpatient procedures. Some radiation treatments or surgical interventions may require overnight monitoring, which our 24-hour facility fully supports.
